newsitem.title: USA: US House panel boosts anti-smoking, food safety.
newsitem.headline: US House panel boosts anti-smoking, food safety.

text.p: A key House panel voted Wednesday to boost funding for Clinton administration anti-smoking and food safety initiatives, but rejected an effort to end crop insurance subsidies for tobacco growers.

On a voice vote, the House Appropriations Committee approved $24.3 million in fiscal 1998 funding for Food and Drug Administration enforcement efforts to reduce teen smoking, up from $15 million approved at the subcommittee level 3 weeks ago and this year's level of $4.3 million.

The move brings the panel closer to the Clinton administration's request of $34 million. The money will be used to enforce an FDA requirement that retailers check photo identification of cigarette customers to verify their age.
But in another voice vote the panel rejected an amendment offered by Rep. Nita Lowey, a New York Democrat, to eliminate federally-subsidized crop insurance for tobacco growers.

"It's very important that we have a consistent policy." Lowey argued, noting that the federal government spends $177 million annually on smoking prevention efforts while subsidizing crop insurance for tobacco growers.
However, opponents argued that the provision would hurt many small farmers who have invested heavily in tobacco production and cannot switch easily to other crops.
"I'm not defending tobacco on the health aspect," said Rep. Bill Hefner, a North Carolina Democrat. But the Lowey amendment is not fair, he said.
The committee took the action as part of its work on the nearly $50 billion agriculture appropriations bill for fiscal 1998, which also passed on a voice vote.

In the area of food safety, the panel restored funding for an undersecretary postion at the U.S. Agriculture Department and provided additional money for a Clinton administration initiative aimed at reducing food-borne deaths and illnesses.

The agriculture appropriations subcommittee under the direction of Rep. Joe Skeen, a New Mexico Republican, had withheld funding for the undersecretary for food safety position in order to prod the administration into formally nominating someone for the post.

Over the weekend, the Clinton administration finally sent its nomination papers for Catherine Wotecki, the current USDA deputy undersecretary for Research, Education and Economics, to the Senate Agriculture Committee.

The full appropriations panel provided $29 million for new food safety surveillance, research and education efforts. That's an increase of $12 million from the subcommittee mark, but still shy of the $43 million requested by the Clinton administration.
